paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial myopathy with lactic acidosis is a mitochondrial disorder. In the patient reported by Saunders et al. (2015), it presented as progressive muscle weakness, hypotonia, seizures, poor weight gain, and lactic acidosis. Muscle from this patient showed degenerating mitochondria with abnormal cristae. Later reports of patients with biallelic PNPLA8 mutations described a broader neurologic spectrum. Nakamura et al. (2024) characterized it as a continuum. At the severe end were developmental and degenerative epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy with congenital microcephaly and pontocerebellar hypoplasia. At the mild end was later-onset neurodegeneration with movement disorder and cerebellar atrophy (Burnyte et al., 2023; Nakamura et al., 2024).

paragraphs.text: Mastaglia et al. (1980) reported a 23-year-old man with a mitochondrial myopathy. He had a high-output circulatory state and cardiomyopathy that led to cardiac insufficiency 22 years before the skeletal myopathy appeared. Venous lactate levels were elevated, and at one stage of the illness he developed severe lactic acidosis. Electron microscopy of muscle showed various mitochondrial abnormalities and an accumulation of neutral lipids, which was confirmed histochemically and by thin-layer chromatography.

paragraphs.text: Saunders et al. (2015) reported a 7-year-old girl (CMH193) who was evaluated for a suspected mitochondrial myopathy with dystonia, abnormal gait, and an abnormal muscle biopsy. She had no symptoms in her first year and met all developmental milestones, although her parents noticed toe-walking. A Gowers sign was present at age 2 years, and by age 3 she could no longer walk. She could sit independently for only 10 minutes because of fatigue. Her fine motor skills declined, and her speech became dysarthric. Muscle weakness was more pronounced proximally. Other findings included tight heel cords, subtle rightward deviation of the tongue, and generalized mildly increased tone. Her symptoms progressed, with increasing proximal weakness and dysmetria. Hypotonicity progressed to spasticity of different opposing muscle groups. She later developed complex partial seizures with recurrent left temporal lobe spikes on EEG. Despite CoQ10 supplementation she did not gain weight and remained very lean. She developed significant lactic acidosis that required bicarbonate supplementation. Creatine phosphokinase was normal, but the anion gap had been consistently elevated since age 5. At 33 months, brain MRI showed subtle increased signal in the medial globus pallidus bilaterally; this was no longer visible 2 years later. Muscle biopsy at 4 years showed variable fiber size with isolated small atrophic fibers of all subtypes and no ragged-red fibers. On electron microscopy, mitochondria showed marked disarray of cristae and globular dense osmiophilic inclusions. There were also subsarcolemmal aggregates of abnormal mitochondria with concentric lamellar membranes, suggesting degenerating mitochondria. Secondary lysosomes containing residual bodies that appeared to be derived from mitochondria were increased.

paragraphs.text: Shukla et al. (2018) reported 2 unrelated girls with biallelic PNPLA8 mutations. Patient 1 was born to consanguineous Indian parents. At birth she had microcephaly (head circumference 29 cm, -4 SD) and a weight of 2,410 g (-2 SD). Multifocal clonic seizures began on the second day of life, and she had spasticity of all 4 limbs and overriding cranial sutures. Brain MRI showed microcephaly with a simplified gyral pattern, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, a prominent cisterna magna with a hypoplastic cerebellum, and brainstem atrophy. MR spectroscopy showed an elevated lipid-lactate peak. Patient 2 was born to nonconsanguineous parents of Indian/Fijian origin. She developed normally until about 13 months of age. She then regressed, with episodes of epilepsia partialis continua and focal seizures that were difficult to control. Her development stagnated at an 8-month level, she was nonverbal, and she needed a gastrostomy tube. She developed acquired microcephaly, with a head circumference at 15 years of 49 cm (-4.7 SD). Other findings included central hypotonia, choreiform movements, dystonia, proximal muscle weakness, absent muscle stretch reflexes, and severe contractures. Serial MRI showed progressive volume loss in the cerebellum, brainstem, and parietal and occipital lobes, along with thinning of the corpus callosum. MR spectroscopy showed a persistently elevated lipid-lactate peak. On electron microscopy, muscle showed enlarged and irregularly shaped mitochondria with surrounding membrane whorls and disrupted cristae, as well as lipid droplets and pools of glycogen. Activities of respiratory chain complexes I through IV were normal. Blood lactate was elevated on several occasions. She also had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with subaortic stenosis, visual evoked potentials with severely reduced amplitudes, elevated growth and differentiation factor-15, and obstructive sleep apnea. The authors noted that Patient 2's presentation was similar to that of the patient reported by Saunders et al. (2015).

paragraphs.text: Burnyte et al. (2023) reported 2 adult sibs with slowly progressive ataxia that began in adolescence. In the brother, symptoms began at age 14 years with weakness and distal muscle atrophy of the lower limbs, accompanied by ataxia and gait disturbance. He needed assistance to walk from age 17 years and became nonambulant at age 44. On examination he had tetraparesis, decreased tone, distal muscle wasting, absent lower limb reflexes, foot deformities, bilateral Babinski signs, marked dysmetria, and length-dependent hypoesthesia. At age 45 years he also had mild dysarthria and horizontal nystagmus. His Mini-Mental State Examination score was 30/30. Nerve conduction studies showed a sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy, and brain MRI showed mild cerebellar atrophy. His sister developed walking difficulty and lower limb weakness at age 14 years. At age 21 she had distal limb atrophy, absent lower limb reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, severe axial ataxia, and appendicular dysmetria. Her cognition was normal, and she had an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Neither sib had visual, auditory, cardiac, or liver involvement.

paragraphs.text: Abdel-Hamid et al. (2024) reported 3 patients from 2 families. Patient 1 had the congenital form of the disease. Patients 2 and 3, from the second family, had progressive microcephaly, infantile-onset seizures, progressive cortical atrophy, white matter loss, bilateral degeneration of the basal ganglia, and cystic encephalomalacia. The authors proposed infantile onset as a new, distinct phenotype. They concluded that PNPLA8-related conditions form a spectrum of overlapping features, with clinical features consistently tracking the age of onset.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) reported 14 individuals from 12 unrelated families with biallelic PNPLA8 variants. Ages at last assessment ranged from 3 days to 33 years. Common features were central hypotonia (13 of 13), dystonia (8 of 12), seizures (10 of 14), and cerebellar atrophy (12 of 12). Eight patients (families 1-8) had a severe phenotype. Their features included congenital microcephaly (5 of 7), global developmental delay with no milestones attained (7 of 7), peripheral spasticity (7 of 8), seizures beginning within 7 months of age (8 of 8), a simplified gyral pattern (6 of 6), pontocerebellar hypoplasia (7 of 7), and severe progressive cerebral cortical atrophy (5 of 5). Four patients (families 11 and 12) had a milder phenotype. All 4 attained walking and had regression of milestones. Three of the 4 had ataxia and mild or no intellectual disability, and seizures were isolated or absent. MRI in this group showed little or no cerebral cortical volume loss but progressive cerebellar atrophy. Two patients (families 9 and 10) were of intermediate severity. Together with 11 previously reported individuals, the authors concluded that PNPLA8-related neurologic disease forms a continuum. It ranges from variable developmental and/or degenerative epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy to childhood-onset neurodegeneration.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) identified biallelic PNPLA8 variants in 14 affected individuals from 12 unrelated families using exome or genome sequencing. There were 14 variants, of which 12 were novel: 4 nonsense, 5 frameshift, 3 intronic variants near exon-intron boundaries, and 2 missense. All had a population frequency of less than 0.001%. Twelve of the 14 individuals carried combinations of nonsense, frameshift, and splice-site variants, which suggested loss of function. In Patient 1, the c.1625+3_1625+6del variant caused skipping of exons 6 through 8, and his fibroblasts showed a significant reduction in the 77-kD PNPLA8 isoform. The frameshift variant p.Glu296LysfsTer6 in Patient 6, who had a severe phenotype, also had a null effect. Two individuals from a separate non-neurologic cohort were homozygous for N-terminal frameshift variants that affect only the 88-kD isoform; one had optic atrophy and the other nonsyndromic hearing loss. In the family with optic atrophy, an affected sib of the proband was heterozygous, and the authors considered the significance of these N-terminal variants undetermined.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) identified a c.1625+3_1625+6del variant in the PNPLA8 gene in a Japanese boy (Patient 1). He had congenital and progressive microcephaly, seizures from day 1, severe developmental delay, a simplified gyral pattern, pontocerebellar hypoplasia, and cerebellar atrophy, and he died at 4 years of age. In his lymphoblastoid cells the variant caused skipping of exons 6 through 8. His fibroblasts showed a significant reduction in the 77-kD PNPLA8 isoform and reduced maximal mitochondrial respiration. Cerebral organoids derived from his iPSCs had fewer basal radial glial cells and upper-layer neurons than organoids from his father's cells.
